asks.plainAsk: Ask for a written warning and time to pay before a late payment counts as breaking the lease.
asks.softerAsk: Could we add a written notice and a short time to pay before a late payment counts as a default?
asks.why: A real lease gives a written warning and time to pay first: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Tenant shall not be in default for failure to pay Rent unless such failure continues for [ten (10)] days after written notice from Landlord.
asks.nextStep: Bring this up first. It decides how fast you could lose the space. If the landlord says no, ask for the fallback.

asks.plainAsk: Ask to get a written warning every time, not just the first few times.
asks.softerAsk: Would you be willing to send a written notice each time, not only the first few times?
asks.why: A real lease gives a written warning before every default: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Landlord shall give Tenant written notice of each failure to pay Rent before such failure becomes an Event of Default.
asks.nextStep: Ask to remove the limit on warnings. A warning only matters if something goes wrong.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the lease's warning come on top of any warning the law gives you, not replace it.
asks.softerAsk: Can we make sure the lease's notice adds to any notice the law requires, instead of replacing it?
asks.why: The law may give you a warning period of its own. This asks that the lease not take it away.
asks.legalWording: Any notice under this Section shall be in addition to, and not in lieu of, any notice required by law.
asks.nextStep: Ask a lawyer what warning the law gives here, then propose the wording below.

asks.plainAsk: Ask to cap your personal guaranty at a set amount, or have it end after the business pays on time for a set period.
asks.softerAsk: Would you consider a cap on the personal guaranty, or having it end after a period of on-time payments?
asks.why: A real lease caps what the guarantor owes: see the example. A cap keeps your own savings apart from the business's debts.
asks.legalWording: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, Guarantor's liability under this Guaranty shall not exceed [$amount].
asks.nextStep: Ask this first, before anything else. It's the clause that can reach your own money. If the landlord won't cap it, ask for the fallback: a guaranty that shrinks or ends over time.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord try to collect from the business before coming to you.
asks.softerAsk: Could the lease say you'll try to collect from the business before coming to me personally?
asks.why: This makes you the backup, not the first person the landlord goes to.
asks.legalWording: Landlord shall first exhaust its remedies against Tenant before seeking payment from Guarantor.
asks.nextStep: Raise it together with a cap on the guaranty.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that your guaranty not cover renewals or changes you didn't agree to in writing.
asks.softerAsk: Can we agree that the guaranty only covers changes I sign off on in writing?
asks.why: A real lease limits the guaranty to the first term: see the example. You shouldn't be bound by changes you never saw.
asks.legalWording: Guarantor shall not be liable for any renewal, extension, or amendment of the Lease unless Guarantor consents to it in writing.
asks.nextStep: Ask that any renewal or change needs your written OK as the guarantor.

asks.plainAsk: Ask to pay only increases above a starting year, or for a limit on yearly increases.
asks.softerAsk: Would you be open to my paying only increases over a base year, or to a yearly cap?
asks.why: A real lease charges only increases above a starting year: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Tenant shall pay Tenant's Proportionate Share of the amount by which Operating Expenses for each year exceed Operating Expenses for the Base Year.
asks.nextStep: Ask the landlord for last year's building costs, so you can see what you'd pay. If the clause can't change, ask for the fallback: a yearly limit.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that major building upgrades, like a new roof, be left out of your share.
asks.softerAsk: Could we leave major projects, like a new roof, out of my share of building costs?
asks.why: Major upgrades last longer than your lease. This asks that you not pay for them.
asks.legalWording: Operating Expenses shall not include the cost of capital improvements, capital repairs, or capital replacements.
asks.nextStep: If the landlord won't leave them out, ask that they be spread over many years, and only for upgrades that lower costs or are required by law. That's how the GBREB form handles them.

asks.plainAsk: Ask for a limit on how far the real amount can go above the estimate, and the right to see the landlord's records.
asks.softerAsk: Would you agree to a limit on how far the actual costs can go over the estimate, and let me see the records?
asks.why: A limit on surprises lets you plan, and seeing the records lets you check the bill.
asks.legalWording: Tenant's share of Operating Expenses for the first Lease Year shall not exceed [110%] of the estimate in this Lease. Tenant may inspect Landlord's records of Operating Expenses on reasonable notice.
asks.nextStep: Ask for last year's actual costs before you sign.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the yearly limit not carry forward, so a slow year doesn't allow a bigger increase later.
asks.softerAsk: Can the yearly limit apply to each year on its own, without carrying unused room forward?
asks.why: A real lease limits yearly increases: see the example. Carrying unused room forward weakens that limit.
asks.legalWording: The limit on increases in Controllable Operating Expenses shall apply each year without carry-forward of any unused amount.
asks.nextStep: Ask that the limit apply to each year on its own.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord need a good reason to refuse.
asks.softerAsk: Would you be comfortable adding that consent won't be unreasonably withheld?
asks.why: A real lease says the landlord can't refuse without a good reason: see the example. Without that, the landlord can block a sale of your business.
asks.legalWording: Landlord's consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed.
asks.nextStep: Ask for this early, especially if you might sell the business someday.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that selling your business, or bringing in a partner, not need the landlord's permission.
asks.softerAsk: Could a change in who owns my business not count as transferring the lease?
asks.why: Selling the business or bringing in a partner is how many small businesses grow or move on. This keeps that from counting as a transfer.
asks.legalWording: A transfer of ownership interests in Tenant shall not be deemed an assignment of this Lease.
asks.nextStep: If the landlord won't drop it, ask that a new owner only needs to show it can pay the rent.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord not be able to take the space back when you ask to transfer the lease.
asks.softerAsk: Could we remove the right to end the lease when I ask about a transfer?
asks.why: Asking for permission shouldn't cost you the space.
asks.legalWording: Landlord shall have no right to terminate this Lease in connection with any proposed assignment or sublease.
asks.nextStep: If the landlord keeps this right, ask that you can withdraw your request and keep the lease.

asks.plainAsk: Ask to be released once the landlord approves the buyer.
asks.softerAsk: Once you approve a buyer, could my business be released from obligations after that date?
asks.why: Once the landlord approves a buyer, the buyer is the one who should answer for the rent.
asks.legalWording: Upon any assignment approved by Landlord, Tenant and any Guarantor shall be released from all obligations arising after the date of the assignment.
asks.nextStep: Ask that the release start on the day of the approved transfer.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord need your agreement to move you, or at least pay for the move and finish the new space first.
asks.softerAsk: Would you agree not to move my business without my consent?
asks.why: A real lease has the landlord pay to move the tenant: see the example. A move can cost you customers who know where you are.
asks.legalWording: Landlord shall not relocate Tenant without Tenant's prior written consent.
asks.nextStep: Ask that any move needs your agreement. If not, ask for the fallback: the landlord pays and finishes the new space first.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord pay all moving costs and finish the new space before you move.
asks.softerAsk: Could the lease say you'll cover the moving costs and have the new space ready before I move?
asks.why: A real lease has the landlord pay the moving costs: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Landlord shall pay all of Tenant's reasonable costs of relocating, and Tenant shall not be required to move until the substitute premises are complete.
asks.nextStep: Also ask that the new space be similar in size and quality.

asks.plainAsk: Ask to remove the landlord's right to end early, or for more notice and repayment of what you spent on the space.
asks.softerAsk: Could we remove the early termination right, or add more notice and repayment for my improvements?
asks.why: A real lease pays the tenant back for its improvements when the landlord ends early: see the example.
asks.legalWording: If Landlord terminates this Lease under this Section, Landlord shall give at least [twelve (12) months'] notice and pay Tenant the unamortized cost of Tenant's improvements to the Premises.
asks.nextStep: Ask for more notice first, then for repayment of what you spent on the space.

asks.plainAsk: Ask for more time to refill the deposit.
asks.softerAsk: Could I have more time to refill the deposit if you ever draw on it?
asks.why: A few days may not be enough to find the money.
asks.legalWording: within [thirty (30)] days after written demand
asks.nextStep: Ask for the time you'd realistically need, such as 30 days.

asks.plainAsk: Ask for a rent reduction if a service is out for more than a few days for reasons the landlord controls.
asks.softerAsk: If a service is out for more than a few days for reasons you control, could the rent be reduced?
asks.why: A real lease makes the landlord responsible for outages it causes: see the example.
asks.legalWording: If any utility or service is interrupted for more than [three (3)] consecutive business days for reasons within Landlord's reasonable control, Rent shall abate until service is restored.
asks.nextStep: Ask how often services have gone out in the building.

asks.plainAsk: Ask for a rent reduction if a service is out for more than a few days.
asks.softerAsk: Could rent be reduced if a service is out for more than a few days?
asks.why: A real lease limits the tenant's risk from outages: see the example. Rent should go down when you can't use the space.
asks.legalWording: If any utility or service is interrupted for more than [three (3)] consecutive business days, Rent shall abate until service is restored.
asks.nextStep: Ask what backup the building has for power and water.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that you only have to remove changes the landlord names in writing when it approves them.
asks.softerAsk: Could I only be required to remove changes you name in writing when you approve them?
asks.why: A real lease limits removal to the changes the landlord names: see the example. Then you know your move-out costs from the start.
asks.legalWording: Tenant shall have no obligation to remove any improvements except those Landlord designates in writing at the time it approves them.
asks.nextStep: Each time the landlord approves a change, ask it to say in writing whether you'll need to remove it.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that rent stop while the space is unusable, and that you can end the lease if repairs take too long.
asks.softerAsk: Could rent stop while the space can't be used, and could I end the lease if repairs take too long?
asks.why: A real lease stops rent while the space is being rebuilt: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Rent shall abate while the Premises are untenantable. If the Premises are not restored within [180] days after the casualty, Tenant may terminate this Lease.
asks.nextStep: Ask what insurance the landlord carries to rebuild.

asks.plainAsk: Ask that the landlord's lender promise to keep your lease if it takes over the building.
asks.softerAsk: Could you get a non-disturbance agreement from your lender, so my lease is protected?
asks.why: A real lease has the lender promise to keep the tenant's lease: see the example.
asks.legalWording: Tenant's subordination is conditioned on Tenant receiving a non-disturbance agreement from each holder of a mortgage on the Building.
asks.nextStep: Ask whether the building has a mortgage now, and ask for the lender's non-disturbance agreement before you sign.

asks.plainAsk: Ask for a way to end the lease early, for example after a set year with notice and a fee.
asks.softerAsk: Would you consider an early termination option, with notice and a fee?
asks.why: Businesses change. A way out with notice and a fee limits what closing could cost you.
asks.legalWording: Tenant may terminate this Lease effective at the end of the [third] Lease Year by giving at least [six (6)] months' written notice and paying a termination fee of [$amount].
asks.nextStep: Decide the earliest year and the most you could pay to leave, then ask.
